dryRun.title: Which query should a test use? (Testing Library priority)
dryRun.note: "The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they give you." Query like a user (roles, labels, text), interact through events, and assert on what the user sees, not on state or internal methods. Bonus: role-based queries force accessible markup.

think.q: Best query for the submit button labelled "Log in"?
why: Role + accessible name is how users and screen readers find it.

think.q: Which should you use to assert that an element is NOT on the page?
why: getBy throws when missing; queryBy returns null so you can expect(…).toBeNull().

think.q: Why not assert on a component's internal state value?
opts: Refactoring the internals breaks the test although the user sees no difference
why: Test behaviour; let internals change freely.

think.q: How do role-based queries improve the app itself?
opts: If the test cannot find a button by role and name, a screen reader user cannot either: they push you to accessible markup
They do nothing for the app
why: Tests become an accessibility check.

think.q: user-event vs fireEvent?
opts: user-event simulates full interactions (focus, keydown, input, keyup…) and is closer to real use; fireEvent dispatches one event
why: This course uses fireEvent to keep setup small; prefer user-event in real projects.

try.task: Write an accessible LoginForm({ onLogin }) that these role/label-based tests can drive: labelled "Email" and "Password" inputs, a "Log in" button, and an error message with role="alert" ("Email and password are required") when either is empty.
try.hint: Wrap inputs in <label> (or use htmlFor/id). Keep values in state; on submit validate and call onLogin({ email, password }).

checks.t: fields and button are reachable by label and role
shows an alert when fields are empty

takeaway.key: Query like a user (role, label, text), interact with events, assert on visible output. getBy throws, queryBy returns null, findBy waits.

dryRun.title: Testing a <Pagination> component
rows: "Next" on the last page is disabled
yes: the contract with the parent
rarely: breaks on every tweak, says little
dryRun.note: Test what a user or a caller relies on: what shows up, what happens on interaction, edge cases (empty, first/last, errors), and the props/callback contract. Skip internals, styling details and giant snapshots. Integration tests of a feature give the best confidence per test.

think.q: Which test gives the most confidence for the least maintenance?
opts: Unit tests of every private helper
An integration test that renders a feature and drives it like a user
why: The "testing trophy": mostly integration tests.

think.q: For a Pagination component, which edge case is most valuable to test?
opts: First and last page (prev/next disabled) and a total of 0
why: Boundaries are where bugs live.

think.q: Main problem with large snapshots?
opts: They cannot be stored in git
They change on every markup tweak and get updated without being read
why: Small, focused inline snapshots can be fine.

think.q: How do you test that a child tells its parent about a change?
opts: Pass a mock function (vi.fn()) as the prop and assert it was called with the right arguments
why: The callback is the public contract.

think.q: 100% line coverage means…
opts: Every line ran during tests, not that the behaviour is correct or the edge cases are covered
why: Coverage shows what is untested, not what is tested well.

try.task: Write Pagination({ total, pageSize, page, onChange }): "Prev" and "Next" buttons (disabled at the ends), one button per page (the current has aria-current="page"), and "No results" when total is 0.
examples: <Pagination total={25} pageSize={10} page={1} onChange={go} /> → pages 1 2 3, Prev disabled
try.hint: pages = Math.ceil(total / pageSize); Array.from({ length: pages }, (_, i) => i + 1).

checks.t: prev disabled on the first page, next on the last
clicking a page calls onChange and marks the current page

takeaway.key: Test behaviour and contracts: what users see, what interactions do, edge cases, callbacks. Skip internals and giant snapshots.
mistakes: Chasing coverage numbers instead of edge cases.

dryRun.title: renderHook(() => useCounter(5))
dryRun.note: renderHook renders a tiny test component that calls your hook and exposes the latest return value as result.current. Wrap state changes in act(); pass changing arguments through initialProps + rerender; use a wrapper for providers. If a hook is only ever used in one component, test that component instead.

think.q: Why wrap result.current.inc() in act()?
opts: act is required for every line
So React processes the update and effects before you assert
why: Testing Library wraps its own events in act; direct hook calls need it.

think.q: You store const { count } = result.current, then call inc() in act. What does count hold?
opts: The old value: always read result.current again after an update
why: result.current is replaced on each render.

think.q: A hook calls useContext(ThemeContext). How do you test it?
why: wrapper renders providers around the test component.

think.q: How do you test that a hook reacts to a changed argument?
opts: renderHook(({ id }) => useUser(id), { initialProps: { id: 1 } }) then rerender({ id: 2 })
why: rerender re-runs the hook with new props.

think.q: When is renderHook the wrong tool?
opts: When the hook is an implementation detail of one component: test the component's behaviour instead
why: Test at the level users (or other developers) use it.

try.task: Write useCounter({ initial = 0, step = 1, max = Infinity } = {}) returning { count, inc, dec, reset }; inc never goes above max; reset goes back to initial. The tests show how to use renderHook, act, rerender and initialProps.
try.hint: useState(initial); inc = () => setCount((c) => Math.min(max, c + step)).

checks.t: starts at initial and counts by step
never goes above max, reset works

takeaway.key: renderHook + act + result.current (re-read after updates), initialProps/rerender for arguments, wrapper for providers.
mistakes: Destructuring result.current once and reading stale values.
Testing hooks that should be tested through their component.

dryRun.title: Testing <Weather city="Pune" /> that calls fetch
rows: intercept HTTP at the network level
slow, flaky: avoid in unit tests
dryRun.note: Mock the edges (network, time, storage), not your own components. Prefer dependency injection or MSW (Mock Service Worker) handlers so your component code runs for real. Always reset mocks between tests.

think.q: Which should you usually NOT mock in a component test?
why: Mocking children hides integration bugs.

think.q: Why is MSW popular for React tests?
opts: It intercepts real fetch/XHR requests, so the component's data code runs unchanged; the same handlers work in the browser
why: Mock at the network boundary.

think.q: You used vi.spyOn(globalThis, "fetch"). What must happen after the test?
opts: Restore it (mockRestore or vi.restoreAllMocks in afterEach) so other tests get the real function
why: Leaking mocks makes tests order-dependent.

think.q: A mock was called. What else is worth asserting?
opts: The arguments it was called with (e.g. the right URL and city)
why: toHaveBeenCalledWith checks the contract.

think.q: How do you test the error state of a data component?
opts: Make the mock reject (mockRejectedValue) or return a 500, then assert the error UI
why: Every async component has an error state worth testing.

try.task: Write Weather({ city, fetchWeather = defaultFetch }): shows "Loading…", then "Pune: 31°C" from fetchWeather(city) (resolves to { temp }), or an alert "Could not load weather" if it rejects. defaultFetch calls fetch(`/api/weather?city=${city}`) and returns the JSON.
examples: tests also spy on global fetch for the default
try.hint: useEffect with an ignore flag; state { status, temp }; .catch sets the error status.

checks.t: default uses fetch with the city in the URL

takeaway.key: Mock edges (network, time, storage), not your components. Prefer injection or MSW, assert call arguments, test error states, restore mocks.

dryRun.title: Waiting for async UI
rows: getBy right after an async action
dryRun.note: Async UI needs waiting, not sleeping. findBy* and waitFor retry until success or timeout. For timers, use fake timers and move time yourself (inside act). Never use arbitrary setTimeout delays in tests.

think.q: A list appears after a fetch resolves. Best assertion?
why: findBy waits as long as needed, up to the timeout.

think.q: What should go inside waitFor?
opts: Only the assertion that may need retrying, not side effects like clicks
why: Side effects inside waitFor may run many times.

think.q: Testing a 5-second auto-dismiss toast. How?
opts: vi.useFakeTimers(), render, act(() => vi.advanceTimersByTime(5000)), assert it is gone
why: Fake timers make time-based tests instant and deterministic.

think.q: "An update to X inside a test was not wrapped in act(...)". Usual cause?
opts: A state update happened after the test stopped waiting (e.g. a fetch resolved later)
why: Await the result (findBy/waitFor) so the update happens inside the test.

think.q: A test passes locally and fails in CI sometimes. Common async reason?
opts: It relies on timing (fixed sleeps) instead of waiting for a condition
why: Wait for state, not for time.

try.task: Write useAsync(fn, deps) returning { status, data, error } (status: "loading" | "success" | "error"), ignoring results that arrive after deps change or unmount. Then pass the async tests (findBy, waitFor, fake timers).
examples: id changes quickly → only the latest result is kept
try.hint: useEffect: set loading, call fn(), use an ignore flag in cleanup.

checks.t: ignores a slow old result after deps change (fake timers)

takeaway.key: Wait for conditions (findBy, waitFor), control time with fake timers inside act, and ignore stale async results in your code.
